question: How does a symphony open with almost no sound?
intro: The symphony begins in the dark: eight bars of cellos and basses alone, then a murmur in the violins and a single melody for oboe and clarinet. Stokowski’s 1927 electrical recording moves briskly through the first of the two movements Schubert completed.

sections.label: Exposition · B minor to G major
Recapitulation · the oboe and clarinet tune returns
sections.mNote: second theme returns in D major, not the tonic

cues.title: Eight bars in the dark
cues.text: The symphony opens softly in the strings: cellos and basses alone, pianissimo, for eight bars. This opening idea returns in the coda, where the movement’s last pages recall it.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #73284, p. 1) shows cellos and basses alone in the first bars, marked pp. The report’s opening level is −42.9 dB at 0:00, rising to −21.1 dB by 0:10; a recurrence analysis finds the opening (4.0–17.5 s) again at 550.0–563.5 s.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A murmur, then a song
cues.text: Violins begin a continuous murmur while violas, cellos and basses turn to pizzicato; within a few bars an oboe and a clarinet sing the melody in unison. Eduard Hanslick heard it in 1865 as a gentle cantilena above the calm murmur of violins.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 0:18 (novelty 0.66); the score (IMSLP #73284, pp. 1–2) shows the violin murmur and pizzicato lower strings before the oboe and clarinet entry. Hanslick’s review is quoted in Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article; no entry is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sent to Graz, never played
cues.text: In 1823 the Graz Music Society gave Schubert an honorary diploma. He sent his friend Anselm Hüttenbrenner, one of its leading members, the two completed movements and the start of a scherzo. Hüttenbrenner neither had it performed nor told the society.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article, “Early history”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert). The article calls Hüttenbrenner’s silence curious and notes that it has produced theories.

cues.title: Four bars for horns and bassoons
cues.text: Just after a minute the music pauses for four bars of horns and bassoons, which turn the key towards G major. It is a typically brief Schubertian transition, and it hands the music to the cellos.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 1:08 (novelty 0.74). Wikipedia describes bars 38–41 as a four-bar transition for the horns (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)); the score (IMSLP #73284, printed p. 4) has sounding notes in both the bassoon and horn staves in these bars. The recording is not bar-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cello melody
cues.text: In G major the cellos sing the celebrated lyrical melody, and the violins take it over, over a gentle syncopated accompaniment. It is the second theme, in G major rather than the D major a B minor movement would usually choose.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s analysis describes the second theme in G major, stated first by the cellos and then by the violins over syncopation. The report’s key estimates (D major at 0:50–1:40, r 0.72–0.86) are confused by the shared notes of G and D major and are not used here. A recurrence analysis matches 76.5–109.0 s with 428.5–461.0 s five semitones lower (G to D).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tutti blows and pauses
cues.text: At 1:56 the strongest boundary of the exposition arrives after a hush: a closing group alternates heavy full-orchestra sforzandi with silences and developmental versions of the G major melody. Listen for the gaps as much as the chords.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 1:56 (novelty 1.00), after a quiet window at 1:50 (−26.9 dB; −13.3 dB at 2:00); further boundaries at 2:08 (0.88) and 2:58 (0.96) with a quiet window at 3:00 (−27.0 dB). The description of the group is Wikipedia’s.

cues.title: Why it stopped
cues.text: Schubert began the symphony in 1822 and left two movements and a sketched scherzo, though he lived six more years. Scholars disagree about why. One suggestion is a link with his first illness; another is that he was drawn away by the Wanderer Fantasy.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article: the speculation about his syphilis and about the Wanderer Fantasy is stated there as conjecture, with the observation that it could have been a combination. The article also notes that a complete scherzo exists in piano score.

cues.title: The exposition ends on a pedal
cues.text: The exposition closes with a B pedal in the second bassoon and first horn under a dominant F♯ chord, a gesture Wikipedia compares with the end of the development in Beethoven’s Eroica. No repeat of the exposition appears in this recording.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia notes the pedal at bar 109 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)); the report reads B major at 3:10 (r 0.83) with a boundary at 3:14 (0.65). The score has first and second endings on printed p. 7 (IMSLP #73284); the recurrence analysis finds no repeat of the exposition, so the repeat is not observed. Bars are not aligned.

cues.title: The development opens in E minor
cues.text: In E minor, the subdominant, the introductory motto of the cellos and basses returns very quietly, now arco, after the exposition’s second ending, and the higher strings take it up. Wikipedia notes that opening a development in the subdominant is unusual: it is a key more often kept for the end of a movement.
cues.evidence: Local key reads E minor at 3:20–3:30 (r 0.71–0.72), after a boundary at 3:14 (0.65) and before one at 3:30 (0.74). The score (IMSLP #73284, printed p. 7) puts the quiet arco cello and bass restatement of the introductory motto after the second ending, with the higher strings taking it up; this is not the oboe and clarinet melody. Wikipedia describes the quiet restatement of the opening melody in the subdominant. Bars are not aligned.

cues.title: Trombones take the tune
cues.text: At about 4:10 the trombones take up a dramatic variant of the opening melody over the full orchestra, and the music climbs to a long climax in E minor. The level swells again at 4:50 and 5:00, among the loudest windows of the movement.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 4:10 (novelty 0.97) and a dip to −33.2 dB at 4:30; the loudest windows include 4:55 and 5:05 (−9.8 dB at 4:50, −9.5 dB at 5:00; local key E minor at 4:40–4:50, r 0.70–0.79). The score shows trombones in ff on pp. 8–9 (IMSLP #73284); the entry is not timed.

cues.title: First heard in 1865
cues.text: The two movements were first performed in Vienna on 17 December 1865, conducted by Johann von Herbeck. He added the finale of Schubert’s Third Symphony, a perpetual-motion D major piece, to make the programme complete. The score was not published before 1867.

cues.title: Flutes and oboes lead home
cues.text: After the outburst the sound sinks to a hush, and the flutes and oboes resume the melody to lead into the recapitulation. Listen for the hush at 5:50 and 6:00.
cues.evidence: Level falls to −22.5 dB at 5:50 and −26.0 dB at 6:00 after −11.6 dB at 5:30; the score (IMSLP #73284, p. 11) shows pp flutes and oboes at the end of the development. Wikipedia describes the flutes and oboes resuming their melodic role at this point.

cues.title: The first tune returns
cues.text: At about 6:03 the oboe and clarinet tune comes back over the violins’ murmur, without the eight-bar cello introduction. The recapitulation has begun, and the recording matches the exposition’s melody closely.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 19.0–34.5 s with 363.5–379.0 s (offset 344.5 s, no transposition, similarity 0.96); boundaries at 6:00 (0.55) and 6:16 (0.60); the score (IMSLP #73284, p. 12) shows the oboe and clarinet over the violins’ murmur. The first bar is not aligned.

cues.title: The cello tune in D major
cues.text: About 7:08 brings the second theme back, now in D major, the relative major, instead of the expected tonic. It has the same shape a fourth lower than in the exposition, brighter against the B minor around it.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 76.5–109.0 s with 428.5–461.0 s at a transposition of five semitones down (G to D; similarity 0.92); the key estimate reads D major at 7:10 (r 0.83). Wikipedia states that the second theme is restated in D major.

cues.title: B major, then a turn
cues.text: Around 8:10 the estimates settle on B major for about half a minute, the major form of the home key, which Wikipedia says closes the recapitulation. The coda will return to B minor.
cues.evidence: Local key reads B major at 8:10–8:30 (r 0.81–0.88) and 9:00 (0.82); the level climbs to −10.9 dB at 8:30. Wikipedia describes the return to the parallel major to close the recapitulation.

cues.title: The opening comes back
cues.text: The coda, in B minor, recalls the opening theme in the low strings and reworks it dramatically on the way to the closing chords. The recording matches the first bars of the symphony at about 9:10.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 4.0–17.5 s with 550.0–563.5 s (offset 546 s, no transposition, similarity 0.91); boundaries at 8:58 (0.63) and 9:26 (0.80). The reworking is described by Wikipedia.

cues.title: Stokowski in 1927
cues.text: Mark Obert-Thorn writes that this was Stokowski’s second recording of the symphony, after an acoustic one in 1924, and that the electrical process better conveys the burnished sheen of the Philadelphia strings. Reviewers hear a swift reading with swooped string phrases.
cues.evidence: Pristine Classical PASC 483 producer’s note and reviews (https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc483). The note concerns Pristine’s own restoration, not this Internet Archive transfer.

cues.title: Emphatic chords, then silence
cues.text: One of the loudest windows of the whole recording comes at 9:45, and the movement ends on emphatic chords. Listen for the last bars and the sound fading after them.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows include 9:45 (−9.8 dB at 9:40; key estimate B minor); level is −14.6 dB at 10:00 and −20.3 dB at 10:20; the file ends at 10:28. Wikipedia refers to the emphatic concluding chords; the release of the last chord is not timed.

transitions.title: A pedal, then a hush in E minor
transitions.how: The exposition ends on a tonic B pedal held in the second bassoon and first horn under a dominant F♯ chord, so the home key waits underneath the harmony that points to it. After the second ending the development begins very quietly in E minor, the subdominant, with the introductory motto in the cellos and basses, which the higher strings then take up. A sudden drop in level makes the join audible.
transitions.evidence: Level falls to −27.0 dB at 3:00; B major reads at 3:10; boundary at 3:14 (0.65); E minor reads at 3:20–3:30. The pedal at bar 109 is described by Wikipedia; the quiet E minor restatement of the cello and bass motto is read from the score (IMSLP #73284, printed p. 7). Bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Flutes and oboes lead the way back
transitions.how: The development’s outburst falls away, through pianissimo figures for flutes and oboes, into a hush. Then the oboe and clarinet tune returns over the violins’ murmur and pizzicato lower strings, as at the start but without the introduction in the cellos and basses. Schubert makes the return quiet instead of triumphant, which keeps the symphony’s mood of unease.
transitions.evidence: Level falls from −11.6 dB at 5:30 to −26.0 dB at 6:00; a recurrence analysis matches 19.0–34.5 s with 363.5–379.0 s; boundaries at 6:00 (0.55) and 6:16 (0.60). The orchestration is read from the score (IMSLP #73284, pp. 11–12); the bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: B major gives way to the recalled opening
transitions.how: The recapitulation modulates back to B major, the major form of the home key, and then the coda returns to B minor with the opening theme in the low strings, the first sound of the symphony. Schubert works it over dramatically on the way to a series of emphatic concluding chords, so the end of the movement is also a return to its beginning.
transitions.evidence: Local key reads B major at 8:10–8:30 and 9:00 and B minor from 9:30; a recurrence analysis matches 4.0–17.5 s with 550.0–563.5 s (offset 546 s); boundaries at 8:58 (0.63) and 9:26 (0.80). The description of the coda follows Wikipedia; bars are not aligned.

source.title: Schubert, Symphonie in H moll (unvollendet), Schubert’s Werke, Serie 1 Nr. 8 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1885)
source.locator: IMSLP #73284, I. Allegro moderato, printed pp. 1–18; timings follow the report’s boundaries and the recurrence analysis and are approximate.

timeline.note: Cellos and basses alone, pianissimo, begin the symphony.
The violins murmur; violas, cellos and basses pluck beneath.
Oboe and clarinet sing the melody in unison over the murmur.
Four bars for horns and bassoons turn the key towards G major.
Cellos, then violins, sing the G major melody over syncopated strings.
Full-orchestra sforzandi alternate with pauses in the closing group.
Development: the introductory motto returns very quietly in the cellos and basses, and the higher strings take it up.
Trombones take a variant of the opening melody over the full orchestra.
Flutes and oboes resume the melody at the end of the development.
Recapitulation: oboe and clarinet over the violins’ murmur, as before.
Coda: the opening theme recalled in the low strings.

fields.note: Bolig dates all three sides of the first movement (CVE-29052, -29053 and -29054) to 28 April 1927. The Internet Archive description and Pristine give the two session days (28 and 30 April 1927) for the symphony as a whole.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Stokowski’s earlier acoustic recording of 1924 used the same matrix numbers without the CVE prefix and different issue numbers (Bolig lists 74894–74897 and 6459–6460); this transfer is the electrical recording of 1927 by its description, session dates and Victor numbers.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive description says “Originally issued as Victor 6663, 6664 & 6665. (Later as a set as M-16.)”; Pristine gives the same numbers and album. Bolig also lists later Victor and HMV issues of the same sides. The disc and side on which the movement boundary falls are not identified; the allocation of matrices to movements follows Bolig’s part numbers.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Parts 1–3: CVE-29052, take 6; CVE-29053, take 6; CVE-29054, take 6
fields.note: Bolig and the Pristine producer’s note agree on the matrices and takes of the first movement. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive description reads “Transfer by Bob Varney”.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was added on 24 January 2011, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The stylus, equalisation, speed and noise treatment are not documented. The file runs 10:28; Pristine’s own restoration runs 10:33, so the two transfers differ by a few seconds, and where the side joins fall in this file is not known.

The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence. The recording was published after 1925, so a US public-domain basis is not established.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
